title: Securing a Flask API with JWT and rate limiting
body: Our internal Flask service started life as a quick prototype: a handful of REST endpoints, no authentication and a single SQLite file. When other teams began calling it we had to harden it fast. This post walks through what we changed. First, every endpoint now requires a JSON Web Token issued by our identity provider. We verify the signature, the expiry and the audience claim in one decorator, so a new route cannot forget the check. Second, we added rate limiting per API key with a sliding window, which stopped a misconfigured cron job from hammering us at 50 requests per second. Third, we validate every request body with Pydantic models and return one consistent error shape with a clear message. Finally we wrote a short threat model: who can call the API, what they can read, and what happens if a token leaks. None of this is exotic, but together it turned a toy into a service we trust.

title: Why our Kubernetes pods kept restarting (and the fix)

Why our Kubernetes pods kept restarting

For two weeks our checkout service restarted every few hours. The pods showed OOMKilled, so the obvious guess was a memory leak in the application. It was not. The container memory limit was 512 MB, but the JVM inside it was sizing its heap from the node's total memory, not from the container limit.

We fixed it in three steps. We set explicit heap flags so the runtime respects the cgroup limit, we raised the limit to match real peak usage measured with kubectl top, and we added a readiness probe so traffic only reaches pods that have finished warming up. We also added an alert on restart count in Grafana so the next problem shows up in minutes, not weeks.

The lesson: when a container dies, read the events and the limits before you blame the code.

title: Building a RAG assistant over our support docs
body: Our support team answers the same fifty questions every week, so we built an assistant that reads our help centre and drafts replies. The design is retrieval-augmented generation. We split every help article into chunks of about 300 words, embed each chunk with a sentence embedding model and store the vectors in Postgres with pgvector. When a question arrives we embed it, fetch the eight closest chunks and pass them to a large language model with a prompt that says: answer only from these sources and cite them. The hardest part was not the model. It was evaluation. We collected 120 real questions with known good answers and measured how often the retrieved chunks contained the answer at all. Improving chunking and adding article titles to each chunk raised that number from 61 to 84 percent. Only then did prompt tweaks matter. Agents can come later; good retrieval comes first.

title: From useEffect spaghetti to server components in Next.js
body: Our dashboard had grown into a forest of useEffect hooks that fetched data, set loading flags and raced each other on every navigation. Moving the data fetching into React server components in Next.js removed most of that code. Each page now fetches on the server, streams HTML to the browser and only ships JavaScript for the parts that are actually interactive, like filters and charts. We typed every server action with TypeScript and Zod, so a wrong payload fails at the boundary with a readable message. The results after a month: 38 percent less client JavaScript, a faster first paint on slow phones and far fewer flickering loading spinners. The migration was not free. Some third-party components assumed they ran in the browser and had to be wrapped as client components, and our tests needed a new setup. But the code is easier to read, and new team members understand where data comes from.

title: Indexing strategies that cut our Postgres query time by 90 percent
body: Our orders page took four seconds to load for large customers. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan over 30 million rows, filtered by customer and sorted by date. A composite index on customer_id and created_at turned the scan into an index range scan and the query dropped to 40 milliseconds. We then looked for other slow queries with pg_stat_statements and found two more patterns worth sharing. First, a partial index on orders that are still open is tiny and serves the most frequent query in the app. Second, an index on an expression, lower(email), let our case-insensitive login lookup use an index again. We also removed three indexes nobody used, which made writes faster. Indexes are not free: each one costs disk space and slows inserts. Measure the real queries first, add the smallest index that serves them, and check the plan again afterwards.

title: What I wish I knew before my first senior developer interview
body: Last year I interviewed for senior roles at six companies and got two offers. The coding rounds were not what made the difference. What mattered was how I talked about past work: the trade-offs I chose, the mistakes I made and what I would do differently. Interviewers wanted to hear how I handled an outage, how I disagreed with a manager and how I helped a junior colleague grow. I prepared five stories in advance, each with the situation, my decision and a measurable result, and reused them across rounds. I also asked better questions back: how decisions get made, how on-call works, and what the team is worried about. Salary negotiation felt awkward, but asking for the range early saved everyone time. If you are aiming for a promotion or a new job, start writing your stories down now, while you still remember the details.

title: End-to-end testing a checkout flow with Playwright
body: Unit tests told us every function worked, yet customers still hit a broken checkout twice in one quarter. We added a small suite of end-to-end tests with Playwright that drives a real browser through the flow: add an item, apply a discount code, pay with a test card and see the confirmation page. Three rules kept the suite fast and trustworthy. Each test creates its own user and data through the API, so tests never depend on each other. We select elements by role and label, never by CSS class, so a redesign does not break them. And we run the suite on every pull request in parallel across four workers, which keeps it under three minutes. Flaky tests are quarantined the same day with an owner and a deadline. The suite has caught four real bugs before release, including a currency rounding error in the discount code path.

title: Offline-first notes in a Flutter app
body: Our note-taking app has to work on the train, in lifts and on bad hotel Wi-Fi, so we rebuilt it offline-first in Flutter. Every change is written to a local SQLite database on the phone first and shown to the user immediately. A background sync job pushes changes to the server when the network returns and pulls changes made on other devices. Conflicts are the interesting part. We store a timestamp and a device ID with every edit and merge at the level of individual fields, so editing a title on one phone and the body on another does not lose either change. On Android we schedule sync with WorkManager and on iOS with background fetch, wrapped behind one Dart interface. Battery use stayed flat in our tests, and support tickets about lost notes went to zero.

title: Shipping a Rust service to AWS Lambda with GitHub Actions
body: We rewrote a hot image-thumbnail endpoint in Rust and now run it on AWS Lambda. Cold starts dropped from 900 milliseconds with our old Node.js version to under 40 milliseconds, and memory use fell enough to halve the monthly bill. The function reads the original from S3, resizes it with the image crate and writes the thumbnail back, all with async code on tokio. Deployment is fully automated. A GitHub Actions workflow runs cargo test and clippy on every pull request, builds a release binary for the Lambda ARM runtime with cargo lambda, and deploys with infrastructure as code when the branch is merged. We kept the service small on purpose: one function, one job, clear metrics. The main trade-off is that fewer people on the team read Rust comfortably, so we wrote a short guide to the codebase and pair on every change for now.
